performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: The first movement of Scheherazade, Op. 35, opens with a phrase for brass and strings, followed by a solo violin over a harp, representing the Sultan and Scheherazade. Pierre Monteux conducts the San Francisco Symphony, with Naoum Blinder playing the solo violin part.

sections.label: Intro · Brass and strings in unison
sections.mNote: The Sultan’s descending phrase, marked Largo e maestoso.

sections.label: Frame · Violin over harp chords
sections.mNote: The violin’s winding recitative introduces Scheherazade.

sections.label: A · Strings, Allegro non troppo
sections.mNote: Allegro non troppo; rolling accompaniment beneath the long tune.

sections.label: B · Horn and woodwind solos
sections.mNote: Horn and woodwind solos follow the full-orchestra passages.

sections.label: Dev · Strings and brass return
sections.mNote: The sea theme builds above the moving strings.

sections.label: A′ · Sea theme returns
sections.mNote: The broad theme sounds over the rolling accompaniment.

sections.label: Coda · E major, wind and strings
sections.mNote: Wind chords and pizzicato strings close the movement.

cues.title: Opening phrase in octaves
cues.text: Brass, low woodwinds and strings play a descending phrase in octaves, marked Largo e maestoso. The strings are marked pesante. Pauses break up the phrase, and soft wind chords follow.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, pp. 1–2: Largo e maestoso, strings marked pesante, and the quiet wind chords. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo violin and harp
cues.text: After the heavy orchestral opening, the solo violin, Scheherazade’s theme, plays above the harp. The score marks the passage Lento and Recitativo. Naoum Blinder is the soloist.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2: Lento, Recitativo, solo violin and harp. Blinder is credited in the recording documentation: https://archive.org/metadata/Sheherazade/metadata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegro non troppo, sea theme
cues.text: Allegro non troppo. The strings begin a rolling accompaniment, and the Sultan’s phrase returns as the broad sea theme. Its long notes are held over the quicker motion below.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2 onwards. Paul Serotsky describes the opening motto’s transformation into the sea music: https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Naval career
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov entered naval college at twelve. He began his First Symphony before a three-year voyage, and on his return divided his life between music and the navy. For years his posts included inspecting naval bands.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, LA Philharmonic programme note, documents the naval training, voyage, First Symphony and band-inspection work. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement

cues.title: Scheherazade and the Sultan
cues.text: In The Thousand and One Nights, Scheherazade leaves each story unfinished at the end of the night. The Sultan postpones her execution so that he can hear the rest. Rimsky-Korsakov gave her a solo violin, which plays against the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass, LA Philharmonic programme note, explains the framing tale and the solo violin’s association with Scheherazade. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade

cues.title: Recording, San Francisco, March 1942
cues.text: Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony made this recording at the War Memorial Opera House on 3–4 March 1942. Naoum Blinder played the violin solos. The complete suite filled Victor’s 78-rpm album DM-920.
cues.evidence: The original transfer documentation gives the venue, sessions, performers and Victor album number. https://archive.org/metadata/Sheherazade/metadata

cues.title: Return of the sea theme
cues.text: The broad sea tune returns over rolling string figures. Brass and strings now play the melody, which first appeared as the Sultan’s unaccompanied theme. Beneath its long notes the accompaniment rises and falls.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, later return of the Allegro material; Serotsky describes the alternating orchestral crests and quieter solo episodes. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing pages in E major
cues.text: The closing pages are in E major. Short solo phrases continue in the strings and winds. At the end a solo cello plays a rising and falling figure under held wind chords, and the strings finish with soft pizzicato notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, closing pages, especially p. 23: solo cello, sustained winds and pizzicato strings. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Wind chords before the violin recitative
transitions.from: Intro · Brass and strings in unison
transitions.how: The heavy opening stops. Soft wind chords, separated by fermatas, lead to the violin’s Lento recitative. Harp chords replace the orchestral bass, and the violin climbs into its winding espressivo line.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement, pp. 1–2, from the opening wind chords to Lento, Recitativo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf

transitions.title: From violin cadenza to Allegro non troppo
transitions.how: A cadenza and a held violin note end the recitative. At Allegro non troppo the key signature changes to E minor. Violas and cellos begin rolling figures, the violins take up the broad tune above them, and the winds sustain the harmony.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2, the end of the violin cadenza and opening Allegro non troppo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, I, full-score scan
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–2: the opening phrase, wind chords and violin recitative; pp. 10 and 18: piccolo, brass and timpani with the sea tune; pp. 21–23: closing wind chords, solo cello and plucked strings.

timeline.note: Low winds, brass and strings state the heavy opening phrase in octaves.
Quiet woodwind chords answer the opening phrase, with pauses between them.
The solo violin begins its recitative above harp chords.
At the Allegro non troppo, the violas and cellos play the wave figures beneath the violin tune.
Piccolo, brass and timpani join the winds and strings as the sea tune grows.
Woodwind solos enter between the string phrases.
High winds, brass and timpani reinforce the strings’ rolling accompaniment.
The brass stops, and solo wind instruments play, answered by the strings.
The sea tune returns with the strings, winds and brass.
The wind hold chords above the continuing motion in the strings.
A solo cello plays beneath held woodwinds; plucked string chords complete the E-major cadence.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and professor, known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
